newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli-PLO talks on Hebron go down to the wire.
newsitem.headline: Israeli-PLO talks on Hebron go down to the wire.

text.p: Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu and the Palestinians' Yasser Arafat scheduled a midnight summit at their border on Tuesday to try to nail down an elusive deal to extend Palestinian rule to the West Bank town of Hebron.
Israeli and Palestinian peace teams met at a Jerusalem hotel, aiming to resolve four disputes still holding up Israel's withdrawal from 80 percent of Hebron.
"The chance that we will finish this evening exists but it is not guaranteed," Prime Minister Netanyahu told reporters in Jerusalem.

U.S. Middle East mediator Dennis Ross said Netanyahu and President Arafat would meet at the Erez crossing between Israel and Gaza at midnight (2200 GMT) in an effort to complete the deal after months of negotiations.

Hebron, a West Bank flashpoint, is home to 400 militant Jewish settlers and 100,000 Arabs. It was due to be given self-rule 10 months ago but violence, security concerns and Israel's change of government in June delayed the pullback.
By sealing the Hebron deal Netanyahu will be doing what he and his right-wing Likud party said they would never do -- cede part of the biblical Land of Israel to Palestinians.

"The agreement is a suicide pact," David Wilder, a spokesman for Hebron's settlers, told Reuters. "It's like having somebody hold a gun to your head and having somebody else helping to pull the trigger."

The settlers made a last-minute appeal to Netanyahu not to meet Arafat or initial the deal. The Israeli leader also faces something of a rebellion from cabinet ministers who oppose the deal -- at least seven out of 18.
"I think Netanyahu has a solid majority for the agreement," his communications chief David Bar-Illan told CNN television. "Most ministers will vote for it."

Hebron is holy to Moslems and Jews who regard the Tomb of the Patriarchs as the burial place of the biblical Abraham. The tomb, the town's Jewish enclaves and about a fifth of Hebron's Arabs will remain under Israeli control.

Palestinian police will deploy in the rest of Hebron, the last of seven Palestinian towns that were to be turned over to Palestinian self-rule under a 1995 interim peace accord signed by the previous Israeli government.
Arafat's adviser Nabil Abu Rdainah told Reuters: "The remaining issues (on Hebron) are very silly. They could be overcome very quickly."
Netanyahu's spokesman Shai Bazak would not discuss remaining difficulties, but PLO officials charged the talks were stuck on:
- Israel's demand the Palestinian Authority extradite to Israel Arabs wanted by the Jewish state.
- Israel's demand for a veto over the names of all PLO police set to serve in Hebron.
- Israel's insistence the PLO promise to crack down on militant groups.
- A dispute over Palestinian control of Hebron's al-Ibrahimi mosque, part of the Tomb of the Patriarchs.
Jordan's King Hussein broke a deadlock on Sunday, nudging the sides toward a compromise timetable for three further Israeli withdrawals from rural West Bank areas now due to be completed by mid-1998.
